steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Opening traps look like free material. Which ones really occur, and how do you tell a trap from a gift? By the end you can run three checks before any capture: where can my capturing piece go, what does the capture leave undefended, and which enemy pawn can hit me with tempo? You can also say when a trap is worth learning at all. [I] The three checks are my own working list, not a published rule.

steps.text: **What makes the cage.** [I] Three features work together. One: a Black pawn on b5 covers both a4 and c4, so one pawn guards both exits. Two: White's own pawns on a2 and c2 shut off the other two diagonal squares. Three: the pawn on c5 hit the queen with tempo, so White never had a free move to rescue the bishop. Remove one feature and there is a hole. Count the exits and who guards each.

**How often do players walk into it?** [V] The Week in Chess files hold 3,370,649 games (2012 to 2026, not de-duplicated, all strengths). about 132,000 begin with the Ruy Lopez, and 285 of them reach this position. White then chose c3 in 106, Bd5 in 98, the queen grab in 43 and a4 in 22. After the grab Black won 35, drew 4 and lost 4. In only 2 of the 43 were both players rated 2500 or more.

steps.text: **A tie to the queen is a tie of cost, not of law.** [I] The black knight on e7 may legally move, because the king is not behind it. But if it moves, the bishop takes the queen. So the knight is tied to e7 as long as the queen stands on d8 and the bishop stays on g5. Check the line behind a piece before you move it. The tie disappears when the queen leaves the diagonal, or when the bishop is traded off.

steps.text: **Is this a pattern or a line?** [V] In the same Week in Chess files, 78 games reach this line after White's knight comes to c3 on move 5. Black chose a bishop to d7 in 46, a knight to f6 in 16 and the pawn push b5 in 7. steps.title: What makes the pawn on e4 safe?
steps.prompt: Predict first. In the second position White's pawn stands on d3. Does the queen fork still bring the pawn back? Then compare.

steps.text: **Count the defenders of your own pawn, too.** [I] A capture is free only if the piece you leave behind can be defended. Here the weak pawn is not the one you take but the one you leave: e4. Before you capture, ask what the queen jump attacks. One defender can be enough: with a pawn on d3, a queen that takes on e4 is captured and the fork fails. With no defender at all, it works.

The pawn recaptures and the h-file is open against White's king.
White tries to cover with the knight.
The queen goes to h4: Black threatens mate.

After 7...Qh4 the engine finds a forced mate for Black (depth 16).

steps.text: **Does this trap ever occur? [V]** The Week in Chess files hold 1 game with the knight on g4 in this line. Our master tree (2500 and above, moves with fewer than 3 games dropped) has no row for it. [I] A trap that nobody plays is not worth a line in your memory. The idea is worth it: before you take a piece that is offered, ask what file or diagonal the capture opens against your own king.

steps.prompt: Teach-back. Write five lines for a friend who has never seen these traps: the idea, when it works, when it fails, one position you could set up on a board, and one warning.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did your five lines say when the trap works? When it fails (the look-alike)? Give an example a beginner could set up with pieces? Name the mistake a hurried player makes? If one is missing, add it. The app grades nothing; a stronger player or a friend can read it.

**Recap.**
- A free pawn is an offer: look at what the capture leaves behind.
- Count the exits of any piece you are about to leave; one pawn can guard two.
- A piece tied to its queen cannot move without losing the queen, even with no king behind it.
- Count the defenders of your own pawn before you take theirs.
- Rare traps teach an idea, not a line.
- The numbers here come from our own files and say what players chose, not what is best.
